title: The Visibility Bargain: The Psychological Costs of Sustained Public Climate Communication
abstract: Abstract: As climate change has moved from a scientific concern to a highly visible societal and political issue, climate scientists have increasingly been called upon to serve as public interpreters of climate risk. Expectations that scientists engage with media, counter misinformation, and participate in public debate have expanded alongside their existing research, teaching, and administrative responsibilities. Yet despite the growing normalization of public engagement as a professional obligation, the psychological consequences of sustained scientific visibility remain insufficiently theorized within psychology. This article provides a conceptual synthesis of psychological and interdisciplinary research to examine the consequences of sustained public climate communication. Integrating research on emotional labor, moral injury, and occupational stress, it introduces the concept of the visibility bargain: an implicit institutional arrangement through which expectations of public engagement redistribute emotional and ethical burdens from institutions to individual scientists. Drawing on qualitative research, case studies, and communication scholarship, the article argues that for climate scientists, sustained public visibility may be associated with cumulative emotional strain, ethical dissonance, exposure to harassment, and career vulnerability. The visibility bargain is proposed as an integrative framework that explains how these distinct forms of strain become concentrated within individual scientists under conditions of expanding public visibility and limited institutional support. The article outlines implications for psychological research, institutional design, and climate communication practice, emphasizing the need to move from visibility-driven models of public engagement toward sustainability-oriented approaches that integrate communication into workload recognition, professional role design, and institutional support structures. By conceptualizing climate communication as a shared institutional responsibility rather than solely an individual professional obligation, the article contributes a psychologically grounded framework for understanding the human consequences of public climate communication.
